newsitem.title: UK: Treasuries steady in London, retain bearish tilt.
newsitem.headline: Treasuries steady in London, retain bearish tilt.

text.p: U.S. Treasuries were stable in London on Thursday following an uneventful Tokyo session but dealers and analysts said the market retained a soft bias.
"The market's going to trade with an offered tone," said a trader at a U.S. bank in London.
He said that while the market was at the low end of a range and had 107-16,18 as a buy zone for the futures, there were still reasons to be downbeat.
"There's a lot of supply sloshing around out there -- all at a loss. And we've got the ECI (employment cost index) on Tuesday to worry about. We'd be better sellers."
June T-bonds at 1021 GMT were trading at 107-25, up 2/32 from Chicago.
The U.S. long bond was at 94-12 mid-price to yield 7.08 percent. That compared with 94-09,12 at the Tokyo finish and 94-10,11 in New York on Wednesday.
The trader said five-years had seen some demand. An auction of five-year paper in New York went better than expected, although Treasuries still finished weak overall afterwards.
"We've seen buying in the five-year sector. It's been deal-related, swap-related as usual in London time," he said.
Economists also said the market looked fragile.
"We've still got the fundamentally bearish bias we've had for some time," said Andrew Bevan, senior bond economist at Goldman Sachs in London. "The economy is growing unsustainably fast."
Bevan said recent data may have been overstating the trend in growth and as a result some of the upcoming numbers could be a little weaker.
"That would be consistent with the idea that we consolidate here. That's obviously what the price action has been telling us for a while."
But he said he would look for opportunities to sell, either on any strength or on a downside break.
The only data of any note on Thursday were help wanted numbers for March. The focus was more on next Tuesday's ECI and then gross domestic product figures after that.

Bevan said Goldman was looking for a 0.9 percent increase in the first-quarter ECI, following a 0.8 percent increase previously. He said that would be consistent with recent average earnings figures and would add to the view that wage pressures were starting to feed through gradually.
